title: Leaders Who Don’t Lead
author: Admired Leadership
summary: A short piece arguing that title and authority do not constitute leadership — action does — and that organisations systematically fail to test for the willingness to act. It catalogues the omissions that define the non-leading leader: no strategic vision, no goals or objectives, no clarified expectations or standards, and no availability as a resource for high performance. The consequences are traced in sequence: teams watched rather than led become discouraged and disengaged, top talent leaves for better opportunities, and those who remain work on a rudderless ship. The piece offers two explanations — either the person lacks the skill and know-how to lead, or they are so taken with title and authority that they have no motivation to move the team forward. Its central move is to reframe leadership as a choice that must be explicitly made rather than a role one is appointed into. The practical proposal is small and concrete: a fifteen-minute conversation asking promising talent to actively decide to become leaders, with the commitment sought before the title is granted. The author claims that people who commit to the idea of being leaders outperform those who merely slip into the role, and closes by paraphrasing Anne Frank on choices making us.
points: The piece's mechanism of harm is sequential rather than dramatic: passive leadership produces discouragement, then disengagement, then the departure of exactly the people the organisation can least afford to lose.
Two distinct failure modes are separated — incapacity and indifference — which matters because only the first is addressable by development.
The core claim is procedural: organisations appoint and hope, when they should require a prospective leader to confront and voice the choice to lead first.
The proposed intervention is cheap and testable — a fifteen-minute commitment conversation used as a screen before the title is conferred.
The asserted payoff is a performance gap between those who consciously commit to leading and those who drift into the role, which is what makes the screening conversation worth the awkwardness.
quotes: Leaders who watch rather than act and establish rules rather than propel change undermine the ability of the team to perform. Over time, team members become discouraged and disengage. The top talent soon leaves for a better opportunity and the remaining team is left to work on a rudderless ship.

Why would a person in the position to lead allow this to happen? Either they’re not ready for the challenge to lead, lacking the skills and know-how to sail the ship, or they are so enamored with title and authority that they have little interest or motivation to move the team forward.

Organizations that fail to appreciate that not all leaders will step up and make the leadership choice typically put people in positions of authority and hope for the best. Sadly, more than a small percentage of selected leaders will choose to focus their attention on personal satisfaction and decline to lead.
All great organizations require every prospective leader to confront the choice to lead and signal they are up to the challenge. The very fact of agreeing to act as a leader can be a game changer.

It's high time organizations of all stripes stop appointing leaders. Ask for their commitment upfront before they are given the title and role. The choice to lead ultimately defines who will and won’t succeed as leaders.
